Core Midland Basin counties like Midland, Martin, and Howard see the tightest well spacing and the deepest buyer pool because operators there are drilling multiple stacked benches on programmed schedules. Move toward the basin edges, into counties like Glasscock's outer reaches or the northern Delaware fringe, and you're in flank acreage where wells are less certain and fewer buyers will compete hard.

Gas-to-oil ratio also shifts the buyer pool. Wolfcamp oil windows in the Midland core draw the broadest bidding. Deeper Delaware Basin intervals run gassier and more overpressured, which narrows the field to buyers comfortable underwriting that production profile and the higher drilling cost that comes with it.

sections.title: What a listing does that a direct offer can't
sections.html:
A direct-sale buyer prices your interest once, against their own model, and asks you to sign. Listing the same interest for competitive bid puts your production history, decline curve, and offset activity in front of the buyer pool at the same time, so each bidder has to price against the possibility that someone else values it higher. In an active basin like the Permian, that difference regularly shows up in the final number.

The tradeoff is fees and time. A broker fee comes off the top of whatever the interest clears at auction or negotiated sale, and running a real process takes weeks rather than the same-day close a direct buyer will dangle. For a producing interest with real cash flow history, that tradeoff usually favors listing. For a small non-producing interest with thin data, a direct sale to a known buyer can still make sense once you've confirmed the offer isn't lowballing activity you weren't told about.

sections.title: Reading your royalty statement before you talk to anyone
sections.html: Your monthly check already tells you which formation is producing, what your net revenue interest is, and how post-production costs are being deducted before you get paid. Any buyer worth talking to will ask for several months of statements before quoting a number, and you should be doing the same math yourself first so you know whether an offer is being pitched against the well's actual decline or against an assumption that you won't check.

faqs.q: Is the Permian still active enough to matter for a small mineral owner?
faqs.a: Yes. Permit and completion activity across Midland and Delaware counties remains among the highest of any US basin, though pace varies bench by bench and year by year with commodity prices.

faqs.q: Does Midland Basin or Delaware Basin sell for more?
faqs.a: Neither side is uniformly higher. Pricing depends on which bench is under your tract, current production if any, and how active nearby operators are that quarter, more than which side of the Central Basin Platform you're on.

faqs.q: What if I only own a small fractional interest inherited from family land?
faqs.a: Small fractional interests still draw buyer interest in the Permian because acquisition desks aggregate many small positions into larger blocks. Your size affects who bids, not whether anyone does.

faqs.q: Should I sell before or after a well is drilled on my tract?
faqs.a: There's no single right answer; pre-drill sales carry more upside and more risk, post-completion sales price against real production data. A broker can model both scenarios against your specific lease terms before you decide.

items.name: Midland Basin Mineral Rights
items.meta: Midland Basin minerals in Midland, Martin, Howard, or Glasscock county sit under the most consolidated, competitively bid acreage in the Permian.

sections.html:
Ownership here has consolidated hard over the past few years. Fewer, bigger operators drilling denser programs changes how a listing process works compared to a scattered basin.

The Midland Basin — Midland, Martin, Howard, Glasscock, Reagan, and Upton counties primarily — is the eastern half of the Permian, and it's become one of the most consolidated pieces of oil and gas acreage in the country. Diamondback's absorption of Endeavor and Exxon's acquisition of Pioneer put a huge share of the core under two operators' drilling schedules, which is a different dynamic for mineral owners than a basin with a dozen mid-size operators competing for permits.

sections.title: What consolidation means for your position
sections.html:
When one or two operators control most of the acreage around your tract, they set the pace of development on their own capital schedule rather than racing competitors for the same rock. That can mean longer waits between spacing units getting drilled, but it also means the operator's plans are more predictable once you know their program — you can often find multi-year development schedules in investor materials that tell you roughly when activity is coming to your section.

For mineral buyers, this predictability is attractive. It's part of why acquisition interest in core Midland counties has stayed strong even as rig counts basin-wide have leveled off from their peak.

sections.title: Spraberry, Wolfcamp, and the stacked-bench math
sections.html:
Midland Basin wells commonly target the Spraberry, Wolfcamp A/B/C/D benches, Dean, and Jo Mill intervals, sometimes from the same pad using different landing zones. That stacking is why a single 640-acre spacing unit can support a dozen or more producing wells over its life, and it's the core reason Midland Basin royalty interests tend to hold value across multiple development phases rather than peaking with one well and declining from there.

Not every bench is economic in every county, though. Glasscock and Reagan see thinner, more selective development than the Midland-Martin-Howard core, and buyer pricing reflects that difference in expected well count.

sections.title: Direct sale offers from acquisition desks
sections.html:
Because the operator landscape is now dominated by a small number of very large, well-capitalized companies, mineral acquisition desks specializing in Midland Basin positions can model future development with more confidence than in a fragmented basin. That confidence sometimes shows up as a genuinely fair direct offer, but it also means these buyers know exactly how much upside they're pricing in, and their opening number rarely reflects the top of that range.

A short listing process, even an informal one where you solicit two or three competing quotes before signing anything, closes most of that gap without the time cost of a full public auction.

sections.title: What to check before signing anything
sections.html: Confirm your net mineral acres against the deed and any prior conveyances — Midland Basin land titles have passed through multiple generations and partial sales in many families, and it's common for owners to underestimate or overestimate their actual interest. Pull recent division order statements if you have production, and check whether your lease terms include a standard one-eighth or a more current one-quarter-plus royalty, since older legacy leases in this basin sometimes carry rates well below current market.

sections.title: Non-operated working interests versus royalty
sections.html: Some Midland Basin owners hold a small non-operated working interest rather than a pure royalty position, typically inherited from an earlier generation that participated in a well's drilling costs directly. A working interest carries both greater upside and real cost exposure to future drilling and operating expenses on the same unit, which is a meaningfully different asset than a royalty interest and should never be valued using the same math. If you're not certain which type of interest you hold, that's worth confirming before any conversation about a sale price, since mixing the two up is one of the more common and costly mistakes owners make when responding to an unsolicited offer. Division order statements and any original participation agreement in your family's records should make this distinction clear if you're uncertain, and it's worth having a landman or broker review those documents directly rather than relying on family memory of how the interest was originally structured decades ago.

faqs.q: Does operator consolidation hurt or help mineral owners?
faqs.a: It cuts both ways. Development becomes more predictable, but you lose the competitive tension of multiple operators bidding for the same drilling slot, which can slow the pace of new wells in some sections.

faqs.q: Which Midland Basin counties are considered core?
faqs.a: Midland, Martin, and Howard counties generally see the densest, most consistent development; Glasscock, Reagan, and Upton are more selective depending on the specific bench.

faqs.q: How many wells can realistically be drilled on my unit?
faqs.a: Stacked-bench development in the Midland core has supported a dozen or more wells per spacing unit in some areas, though this varies widely by county and by which formations are economic there.

faqs.q: Is my older lease royalty rate below current market?
faqs.a: Many legacy Midland Basin leases were signed at one-eighth royalty decades ago, well below rates commonly negotiated today; this affects your net income and should factor into any sale valuation.

items.name: Delaware Basin Mineral Rights
items.meta: Delaware Basin minerals in Reeves, Loving, Culberson, Lea, or Eddy county sit under some of the deepest, most active drilling in Texas and New Mexico.

sections.html:
The Delaware side of the Permian runs deeper, gassier, and more overpressured than its Midland counterpart, and the buyer pool has adjusted to price that difference rather than avoid it.

The Delaware Basin covers the western half of the Permian complex, stretching from Reeves, Loving, Culberson, and Ward counties in Texas across the state line into Lea and Eddy counties, New Mexico. Wolfcamp, Bone Spring, and Avalon Shale sections stack here at depths that often run several thousand feet deeper than equivalent zones in the Midland Basin, which changes both the drilling economics and who's willing to bid on the minerals underneath.

sections.title: Depth changes who shows up to bid
sections.html:
Deeper wells cost more to drill and complete, and the pressure regimes in the Delaware require different casing programs than shallower Midland Basin targets. That raises the operator break-even, which in turn narrows the field of mineral buyers to those comfortable underwriting higher-cost, higher-pressure production. It's still a competitive market — Matador, EOG, Coterra, Devon, and Occidental all run active programs here — but the bidding pool skews toward buyers who specialize in Delaware-specific risk rather than generalists.

New Mexico counties on the Lea and Eddy side see some of the tightest bidding in the entire basin right now, driven partly by state-level permitting stability compared to the regulatory churn some operators have faced in other western states.

sections.title: Gas weighting and what it does to your check
sections.html:
Delaware wells commonly produce a richer gas and NGL stream than Midland Basin wells, which means your royalty check is more exposed to gas price swings than an equivalent Midland interest would be. When gas prices soften, Delaware royalty checks feel it faster and harder than oil-weighted Midland positions, and that volatility is priced into acquisition offers whether or not the buyer says so directly.

It's worth pulling your own statements and separating oil, gas, and NGL volumes line by line before accepting any number. A buyer quoting off headline BOE production without breaking out the commodity mix is quoting against an assumption, not your actual cash flow.

sections.title: Core versus flank inside the Delaware
sections.html: Reeves and Loving counties sit in the thickest, most consistently productive part of the play and see the deepest operator commitment. Move toward Culberson's western edge or the shallower northern Delaware fringe near the Central Basin Platform and well results get more variable, which thins the buyer pool accordingly. Where your tract sits relative to existing laterals and permitted units matters more here than almost anywhere else in the Permian, because the formation quality changes meaningfully over short distances.

sections.title: Listing against direct offers in a technical play
sections.html: Because Delaware Basin economics require more specialized underwriting, a listed sale process can surface real spread between buyers who model the deep pressure regime accurately and those quoting off basin-wide averages. A direct offer from a generalist buyer is often pricing in a discount for uncertainty they haven't bothered to resolve — a targeted listing forces buyers who actually know the local geology to compete on their real numbers instead.

sections.title: Water handling as a cost line worth understanding
sections.html: Delaware Basin wells produce substantial volumes of produced water alongside oil and gas, and managing that water, whether through disposal wells or recycling for future completions, has become a significant part of operator cost structure across Reeves, Loving, and Ward counties in particular. Some operators have built out extensive water infrastructure and midstream partnerships specifically to manage this, and areas with established water handling capacity tend to see more consistent development pace than areas where an operator would need to build that infrastructure from scratch. It's a less obvious factor than well spacing or bench depth, but it's worth asking about if you're trying to understand why development near your tract has moved faster or slower than a neighboring section with what looks like similar geology on paper.

faqs.q: Is Delaware Basin mineral value lower than Midland because of the extra drilling cost?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Higher well costs are offset by strong per-well production in the core, so pricing depends more on your specific location and commodity mix than on which side of the Permian you're in.

faqs.q: Why do New Mexico counties sometimes see more buyer interest than Texas ones?
faqs.a: Some buyers weight New Mexico acreage favorably for permitting consistency, though this shifts with state policy and shouldn't be assumed to hold indefinitely.

faqs.q: How do I know if my tract is core or flank Delaware acreage?
faqs.a: Look at offset well results and permitted units filed near your section through the county clerk or state oil and gas commandate records; a broker can pull and interpret this for you.

faqs.q: Does a gassier well mean a worse deal for me as a mineral owner?
faqs.a: Not automatically. It means your income is more sensitive to gas price cycles, which is a risk factor to understand and price into any sale decision rather than a reason to assume lower value.

items.name: Eagle Ford Shale Mineral Rights
items.meta: Eagle Ford minerals price differently in the Karnes oil window than the Webb County dry gas window. Know which one your county sits in before you sell.

sections.html:
Ask two Eagle Ford mineral owners what their interest is worth and you can get two very different answers, and both can be right, because this play isn't one thing — it's three.

The Eagle Ford runs in a band across South Texas from the Mexican border up through the San Antonio area, and it changes character as it goes. Karnes and DeWitt counties sit in the black oil window. Move southwest into La Salle and McMullen and you're in the condensate window. Keep going toward Webb County near the border and it turns to dry gas. Same formation, three different products, three different buyer pools.

sections.title: The oil window: Karnes, DeWitt, Gonzales
sections.html:
This is where the Eagle Ford boom concentrated its heaviest drilling, and it remains the most consistently bid part of the play. EOG Resources holds a dominant position across much of the oil window and has kept a steady development pace here even as broader Eagle Ford rig counts declined from their peak years. Mineral owners in this window generally see the widest buyer field because the production economics are the most straightforward to underwrite.

Marathon and ConocoPhillips, which absorbed Burlington Resources' legacy position, also hold significant oil-window acreage, so it's common for a single county to have three or four active operators drilling within a few miles of each other.

sections.title: The condensate and dry gas windows
sections.html:
La Salle and McMullen counties sit in a transition zone producing a lighter condensate stream, which trades closer to oil pricing but carries more gas exposure than the core oil window. Development pace here tracks oil prices more loosely and gas prices more than owners sometimes expect.

Webb County and the play's far southwestern extent run dry gas, and that changes the buyer conversation entirely. Dry gas Eagle Ford competes for operator capital against the Haynesville and other gas basins, so activity here rises and falls with gas prices more sharply than the oil window does, and the buyer pool for minerals in this stretch is noticeably thinner.

sections.title: Why your county, not your acreage, drives the offer
sections.html: It's common for an out-of-state heir to receive an offer on Eagle Ford minerals and assume it reflects the play's boom-era reputation without checking which window their specific tract sits in. A Karnes County oil-window interest and a Webb County dry-gas interest can carry very different value even at similar acreage, and a generic offer letter mailed across a wide mailing list won't reflect that distinction. Confirming your exact county and, ideally, your section and township against public GIS mapping before responding to any offer is worth the hour it takes.

sections.title: Listing across a mature but still-active play
sections.html: The Eagle Ford isn't the newest story in Texas oil and gas anymore, but oil-window counties still see meaningful permitting and refracturing activity on older wells, which keeps a real buyer pool interested. A listing process that documents your production history, or lack of it, and clearly states which window your tract sits in tends to draw sharper offers than a blanket direct-mail response, particularly for owners outside the oil-window core who need buyers to actually understand the gas-price sensitivity they're taking on.

sections.title: Refrac activity and what it means for older wells
sections.html: As the Eagle Ford has matured, a growing share of operator activity in the oil window has shifted toward refracturing older wells, reapplying modern completion techniques to locations originally drilled with earlier-generation methods, rather than exclusively drilling new locations. A successful refrac can meaningfully extend a well's productive life and boost near-term output, which shows up directly in royalty payments even without a brand-new well being spudded nearby. If your family's minerals are tied to wells drilled in the play's early boom years, it's worth checking whether refrac activity has occurred or is planned nearby, since that can change the production trajectory you'd otherwise expect from a simple decline curve and materially affect what a buyer should be willing to pay. Texas Railroad Commandate records list completion and refrac activity by lease, so this is a checkable fact rather than something you need to take a buyer's word for.

faqs.q: Which Eagle Ford counties are considered the strongest for mineral value?
faqs.a: Karnes and DeWitt counties, in the oil window, have historically seen the most consistent drilling activity and the broadest buyer interest.

faqs.q: Does dry gas Eagle Ford acreage still attract buyers?
faqs.a: Yes, but the pool is smaller and offers track gas prices more closely; buyers here tend to be gas-focused acquisition desks rather than generalists.

faqs.q: How do I find out which window my county is in?
faqs.a: Public state and county GIS mapping tools show producing well locations and formation targets near your section; a broker can also pull this for you against your specific deed description.

faqs.q: Is the Eagle Ford still being actively drilled?
faqs.a: Yes, though at a lower pace than its early-2010s peak. The oil window in particular continues to see permits, refracs, and infill development from established operators.

items.name: Bakken Mineral Rights
items.meta: Bakken minerals in McKenzie, Mountrail, Williams, or Dunn county still draw strong buyer interest 15+ years into the play. Here's what still matters.

sections.html:
The Bakken kicked off the modern shale-oil era, and unlike some of its contemporaries, it never really went quiet — the core counties are still some of the most competitively bid oil minerals in the country.

The Bakken and underlying Three Forks formations sit under the Williston Basin, with McKenzie, Mountrail, Williams, and Dunn counties in North Dakota forming the productive core. This was the play that proved long-lateral horizontal drilling and multistage fracturing could work at scale, well before the Permian caught up, and Continental Resources, Hess, ConocoPhillips through its Burlington legacy, and Whiting — now part of Chord Energy — have spent over a decade building dense development programs across it.

sections.title: Why McKenzie County sits at the center of it
sections.html:
McKenzie County alone accounts for a large share of North Dakota's total oil production, and it's where operators have pushed lateral lengths the furthest and packed the most wells per spacing unit. If your family's minerals sit in McKenzie or neighboring Mountrail and Williams counties, you're in the part of the basin where multi-well pad development has been the norm for years, which generally means a longer, more predictable production history to price a sale against.

Move toward Dunn County's western edge or the basin's outer fringe and you're in territory where well results get patchier and development has been slower and more selective.

sections.title: The logistics factor unique to this basin
sections.html: Unlike Texas and Oklahoma plays sitting near dense pipeline networks, Bakken production has always depended more heavily on rail and long-haul pipeline to reach refining markets, which means transportation costs and takeaway capacity affect the netback price you're actually getting paid against. When pipeline capacity has been tight in past years, differentials between Bakken wellhead pricing and national benchmarks widened, and that shows up directly in royalty checks even when production volumes hold steady. It's worth understanding your specific gathering and transportation deductions when reviewing a statement.

sections.title: Weather, permitting pace, and what it means for timing
sections.html: North Dakota's winters genuinely slow drilling activity for parts of the year, which creates a seasonal rhythm to permitting and completions that doesn't exist in southern basins. This doesn't change your interest's underlying value, but it can affect how quickly a buyer can get comparable recent transaction data to price against, and it's a reasonable thing to ask about if you're getting offers that seem to reference stale activity.

sections.title: A mature core with real competitive bidding
sections.html: Fifteen-plus years into major Bakken development, this isn't a speculative frontier play anymore, and that maturity works in a mineral owner's favor. There's enough transaction history and production data for buyers to underwrite confidently, which keeps the acquisition market active and competitive in the core counties even as the initial boom-era excitement has faded. A listing process that puts your production history in front of several Bakken-focused buyers at once still tends to outperform a single unsolicited offer, particularly for owners who haven't shopped their interest in several years and may not know current pricing.

sections.title: Three Forks as the second act
sections.html: A meaningful part of what's kept the Bakken's core counties active well past the initial development wave has been operators targeting the underlying Three Forks formation with its own set of horizontal wells, effectively giving many spacing units a second layer of drilling beyond the original Bakken bench. This stacked development is part of why McKenzie and Mountrail county royalty interests have often seen renewed activity years after an owner might have assumed their unit was fully developed. If you haven't checked recent permit filings near your tract in a while, it's worth doing before assuming your production history has already peaked, since a Three Forks well on the same unit can meaningfully change the picture. North Dakota's Oil and Gas Division publishes permit and completion data by section, so this is a straightforward check to run before you assume a producing history is finished growing. A broker who routinely pulls this data for Bakken owners can usually tell you within a day whether additional development near your unit is a realistic near-term prospect or not.

faqs.q: Is the Bakken still being actively drilled?
faqs.a: Yes, particularly in McKenzie, Mountrail, and Williams counties, though the pace has moderated from the boom years as the play has matured into steadier, longer-term development.

faqs.q: Why does pipeline capacity matter for my royalty check?
faqs.a: Bakken crude has historically depended on rail and long-haul pipeline for transport; when takeaway capacity tightens, wellhead price differentials widen and that reduces net royalty income even at steady production volumes.

faqs.q: Does winter weather actually slow North Dakota drilling?
faqs.a: Yes, cold-weather operations genuinely reduce completion activity in parts of the year, creating a seasonal pattern that's worth factoring into how recent an offer's underlying data actually is.

faqs.q: Should I expect the same buyer interest as newer plays like the Permian?
faqs.a: Core Bakken counties still see strong, competitive buyer interest given the play's long production history and data depth, though basin-wide activity is generally lower than the Permian's current pace.

items.name: Anadarko Basin Mineral Rights
items.meta: Anadarko Basin minerals in the Oklahoma and Texas panhandle sit in older, deeper legacy production. Here's what still moves and what's gone quiet.

sections.html:
This is one of the older gas-producing basins in the country, and its mineral market looks less like a boom play and more like a slow, steady legacy income stream with occasional pockets of new activity.

The Anadarko Basin covers the western Oklahoma panhandle and adjoining Texas panhandle counties, with Custer, Washita, Roger Mills, and Beckham counties historically hosting the most concentrated deep-basin production. It's a genuinely old basin geologically, with production dating back decades from formations like the Granite Wash, Cleveland, and Tonkawa, and it overlaps in places with the shallower Mississippi Lime play to the north. The wells here run deep and gas-heavy, which has always kept development more selective than in shallower, cheaper-to-drill plays.

sections.title: Why this basin never had a modern shale boom of its own
sections.html: The Anadarko's productive zones are tight sands and older conventional-style reservoirs rather than the thick, laterally continuous shale sections that drove the horizontal drilling boom elsewhere. Wells here are typically deeper and more expensive to drill than in the SCOOP and STACK plays immediately to the south and east, which have pulled a lot of Oklahoma operator capital toward them instead over the past decade. That's left large stretches of the Anadarko in a maintenance mode: existing wells still producing, but comparatively few new ones being drilled.

sections.title: What your royalty check reflects here
sections.html: If your family has owned Anadarko Basin minerals for a generation or more, your check is most likely coming from wells drilled years or decades ago that have settled into a long, shallow decline curve rather than the steep initial decline of a new shale well. That's actually a more predictable income stream in some ways, since the volatility of a brand-new well's first-year production isn't in play, but it also means the growth story that drives premium mineral pricing elsewhere is largely absent here.

sections.title: Where new activity does still happen
sections.html: Deep gas activity in the Anadarko has never fully stopped; it moves with gas prices more directly than oil basins do, and operators occasionally return to re-complete older wells or drill infill locations in the more productive Granite Wash trend when gas economics justify it. Beckham and Washita counties have seen more of this intermittent activity than the basin's outer edges. It's worth checking recent Oklahoma Corporation Commandate filings for your specific township before assuming nothing is happening near your tract.

sections.title: Selling a mature, quiet interest
sections.html: Buyers for Anadarko Basin minerals tend to be smaller, more specialized acquisition funds that focus specifically on legacy Mid-Continent production rather than the large national players chasing newer plays. The bidding pool is thinner than in an active shale basin, which makes it more important, not less, to get more than one quote before selling, since a single buyer here has more room to lowball a seller who assumes there's no competition at all.

sections.title: Title and unit history worth double-checking
sections.html: Because so much Anadarko Basin production traces back decades, it's common for ownership records to have passed through several generations, partial assignments, and old unit agreements that don't always match a family's current understanding of what they own. Spacing units established under older Oklahoma Corporation Commandate orders may cover different acreage than what a current owner assumes, and it's worth confirming your actual net mineral acres and unit participation against the county clerk's records and any historical division orders before agreeing to a number. A buyer working from outdated or incomplete title information can end up quoting a price that doesn't match your true interest, in either direction, so getting this confirmed independently protects you regardless of which way the mismatch runs. This kind of title cleanup takes a little longer than a quick sale, but for a legacy basin like this one, where you're not racing a drilling permit clock, there's rarely a reason to rush past it. A few extra weeks spent confirming your net mineral acres almost never costs you a real opportunity in a basin moving this slowly, and it protects you from accepting a number built on someone else's guesswork about what you actually own.

faqs.q: Is the Anadarko Basin still producing meaningful gas?
faqs.a: Yes, though mostly from established wells on a long decline curve rather than new drilling; total activity is well below the pace of active shale plays nearby.

faqs.q: Why did SCOOP and STACK get more attention than the Anadarko?
faqs.a: Those plays target thicker, more continuous shale zones that support horizontal drilling economics; the Anadarko's tighter, deeper sands are generally more expensive to develop per well.

faqs.q: Does a mature, low-activity basin mean my minerals are worth less?
faqs.a: It generally means lower speculative upside than an active shale play, but existing production still carries real value based on current cash flow, and that value depends on your specific well's decline stage.

faqs.q: How do I find buyers for a quiet legacy interest like this?
faqs.a: Smaller Mid-Continent-focused acquisition funds are typically more active here than national buyers; getting multiple quotes matters even more in a thin market.

items.name: SCOOP & STACK Mineral Rights
items.meta: SCOOP and STACK minerals in Grady, Stephens, Kingfisher, or Canadian county sit under Continental Resources' home turf. Know the players before you sell.

sections.html:
One company dominates the map here more than in almost any other major US play, and that changes the calculus for what a fair offer actually looks like.

SCOOP stands for South Central Oklahoma Oil Province, covering the Woodford and Springer formations under Grady, Stephens, and Garvin counties. STACK — Sooner Trend Anadarko Basin Canadian Kingfisher — sits to the north, targeting the Meramec and Osage intervals under Kingfisher, Canadian, and Blaine counties. Both plays share one dominant operator: Continental Resources, which built much of its identity around this acreage before going private in 2022, and which still shapes drilling pace and mineral demand across both plays more than any other single company.

sections.title: What a dominant operator means for bidding
sections.html:
Marathon and Devon also hold meaningful SCOOP and STACK positions, so it isn't a single-operator monopoly, but Continental's scale means their capital allocation decisions move the whole play's activity level more than any competitor's. When Continental slows drilling in a county, offset operators often follow rather than filling the gap, which can leave mineral owners in that county facing a thinner buyer pool than the play's overall reputation would suggest.

Going private removed Continental from quarterly public disclosure requirements, which means mineral owners have less visibility into their forward drilling plans than they did when the company reported to public shareholders. That's a real information gap worth accounting for when you're deciding whether to sell now or wait for announced activity.

sections.title: Woodford oil versus Meramec condensate
sections.html: SCOOP's Woodford and Springer targets run oilier in the core Grady and Stephens county acreage, with the play turning gassier toward its southern and eastern edges. STACK's Meramec target produces a richer condensate stream in Kingfisher County, considered the play's core, tapering to drier gas as you move into Blaine and the western STACK extent. As with most Oklahoma plays, the commodity mix under your specific section matters more to valuation than which named play you're technically in.

sections.title: Oklahoma spacing and pooling realities
sections.html: Oklahoma's forced pooling process means an operator can incorporate your minerals into a drilling unit even without your voluntary lease, which is different from how things work in many other states and worth understanding before you sign anything. If you've received a pooling order or a lease offer tied to one, that's a strong signal a well is coming to your section regardless of what you decide, which changes the calculus on whether to sell now versus wait for production history.

sections.title: Getting a real bid in a concentrated market
sections.html: Because Continental's private status limits public information, a listing process that pulls actual Oklahoma Corporation Commandate filings and offset permit data tends to produce sharper offers than relying on whatever a single buyer volunteers. Smaller acquisition funds that specialize in SCOOP and STACK minerals often compete hard for interests that larger buyers overlook, so it's worth casting a wider net than the first call you get.

sections.title: How gas prices have reshaped drilling pace here
sections.html: Both SCOOP and STACK have meaningful gas exposure alongside their oil production, and like most Oklahoma plays, drilling pace has moved with commodity price cycles more visibly than in purely oil-focused basins. During stretches of weak gas pricing, operators have shifted rigs toward the oilier parts of each play, concentrating activity in Grady and Stephens counties for SCOOP and core Kingfisher acreage for STACK, while pulling back from gassier, thinner-margin locations elsewhere. Understanding where your specific tract falls on that oil-to-gas spectrum helps explain why development pace nearby may have sped up or slowed down independent of anything happening with your particular mineral interest, and it's a useful lens for judging whether a current offer reflects the play's present economics or an outdated snapshot from a different price environment. Oklahoma Corporation Commandate production data is broken out by well and available to the public, which makes checking this yourself entirely realistic rather than something you have to take entirely on faith, and a broker working this play regularly should already have that data pulled before ever quoting you a number.

faqs.q: What's the difference between SCOOP and STACK?
faqs.a: SCOOP sits in south-central Oklahoma targeting the Woodford and Springer formations; STACK sits north of it targeting the Meramec and Osage, with somewhat richer condensate production in its Kingfisher County core.

faqs.q: Does Continental Resources going private affect my mineral value?
faqs.a: It reduces public disclosure about their drilling plans, which means less forward visibility for mineral owners, but doesn't inherently change well economics or buyer demand for your specific interest.

faqs.q: What is forced pooling and does it affect me?
faqs.a: Oklahoma allows operators to include unleased minerals in a drilling unit through a Corporation Commandate pooling order; if you've received one, a well is very likely coming regardless of your lease status.

faqs.q: Is STACK oilier than SCOOP or the reverse?
faqs.a: Neither is uniformly oilier; it depends on the specific county and formation bench, with core Kingfisher STACK and core Grady/Stephens SCOOP both running oil-weighted compared to their play edges.

items.name: Haynesville Shale Mineral Rights
items.meta: Haynesville minerals in Caddo, Bossier, DeSoto, or Panola county live and die on gas prices. Here's how that volatility should shape your sale decision.

sections.html:
No basin in this country swings its drilling pace with gas prices the way the Haynesville does. Understanding that rhythm matters more here than almost any other single fact.

The Haynesville sits under northwest Louisiana and the adjoining corner of East Texas — Caddo, Bossier, DeSoto, and Red River parishes on the Louisiana side, Panola, Harrison, and Shelby counties on the Texas side. It's a pure dry gas play, which means unlike an oil basin where royalty checks stay relatively steady, Haynesville income tracks the Henry Hub gas price almost directly, and operators here throttle drilling up and down with that price faster than in almost any oil-weighted basin.

sections.title: The operators and what drives their pace
sections.html: Chesapeake, now operating as Expand Energy after its merger with Southwestern, remains one of the largest Haynesville producers alongside Comstock Resources, Aethon Energy, and a meaningful presence from Southwestern's legacy assets. These companies idled significant drilling during the 2023-2024 gas price collapse and have been bringing rigs back as LNG export demand from Gulf Coast terminals has firmed up pricing. That LNG demand story is arguably the single biggest driver of Haynesville activity right now — proximity to export infrastructure gives this basin's gas a demand outlet that landlocked dry gas plays don't have.

sections.title: Why your royalty check moves so much
sections.html:
If you've owned Haynesville minerals for several years, you've likely watched your check swing by half or more between good gas-price months and weak ones, without any change in the well's actual production volume. That's the nature of a dry gas royalty — you're getting paid a percentage of revenue, and gas revenue is entirely a function of price times volume, with no oil cushion to smooth things out.

This volatility matters directly for a sale decision. A buyer pricing your interest during a gas price trough will offer less than the same buyer would during a strong LNG-demand quarter, so timing a sale against the gas price cycle, to the extent you can, is worth thinking about rather than assuming your interest is worth a fixed number regardless of when you sell.

sections.title: Core versus edge in this basin
sections.html: Caddo and DeSoto parishes in Louisiana, along with the adjoining Texas counties near the state line, sit in the thickest, most productive core of the play and have held operator commitment even through the 2023 downturn. Move toward the northern or western edges of the mapped Haynesville extent and well results get more inconsistent, which is where buyer interest thins out fastest during any price weakness.

sections.title: Listing during a recovering gas market
sections.html: With LNG demand pulling Haynesville activity back up after a rough stretch, this is a basin where a competitive listing process can capture real upside if buyers are actively repositioning for renewed drilling. A direct offer locked in during the recent downturn may not reflect where buyer appetite has moved since, so it's worth getting a current read on the market rather than assuming an old quote still applies.

sections.title: Louisiana versus Texas side differences
sections.html: While the Haynesville is a single formation, the Louisiana parishes and Texas counties that make it up operate under different state regulatory frameworks, different severance tax structures, and in some cases different typical lease terms that have developed over the play's history. Louisiana's parish-based system and Texas's county-based system also mean title research and courthouse records are organized differently depending on which side of the state line your minerals sit, which is a practical detail worth confirming with anyone helping you evaluate an offer, since it affects how quickly ownership and production history can be verified. Louisiana's civil-law property framework also handles some mineral ownership and succession questions differently than Texas's common-law approach, which matters for heirs sorting out inherited interests across the state line. If your family's Haynesville minerals passed through several generations without a clean succession or probate record, that gap can complicate a sale regardless of which side of the state line you're on, and resolving it before listing tends to go faster than trying to fix it mid-negotiation.

faqs.q: Why did my Haynesville royalty check drop so much over the past couple years?
faqs.a: Dry gas royalties track Henry Hub pricing directly, and gas prices fell sharply in 2023-2024, which reduced revenue even where production volumes held steady.

faqs.q: Is Haynesville drilling activity picking back up?
faqs.a: Operators have been adding rigs back as LNG export demand from Gulf Coast terminals has supported gas prices, though the pace still depends on where prices sit.

faqs.q: Does LNG export demand actually affect my mineral value?
faqs.a: Yes, indirectly. Stronger gas demand supports higher prices and more drilling, both of which improve what buyers are willing to pay for producing or undeveloped Haynesville minerals.

faqs.q: Should I wait for gas prices to rise before selling?
faqs.a: That depends on your risk tolerance and cash needs; a broker can walk through recent pricing trends and current buyer appetite so you're deciding with current information rather than guessing.

items.name: Marcellus Shale Mineral Rights
items.meta: Marcellus minerals in northeast Pennsylvania price differently than southwest PA or WV panhandle acreage. Know your gas type before evaluating an offer.

sections.html:
This play splits cleanly into two different markets depending on which corner of Appalachia you're in, and owners who don't know which side they're on tend to leave money on the table.

The Marcellus Shale underlies a huge swath of Appalachia, but it doesn't behave the same way everywhere. Northeastern Pennsylvania counties like Susquehanna, Bradford, and Tioga produce dry gas, with virtually no liquids to add value beyond the gas stream itself. Southwestern Pennsylvania and the West Virginia panhandle counties produce wetter gas rich in natural gas liquids, which typically fetch a better netback than dry gas alone. EQT is the largest operator basin-wide, with Coterra, Range Resources, Antero, and Chesapeake's successor Expand Energy all holding significant acreage across the play.

sections.title: Dry gas northeast versus wet gas southwest
sections.html:
If your minerals sit in Susquehanna or Bradford County, your royalty check is a pure play on Henry Hub gas pricing and whatever basis differential applies to gas moving out of northeastern Pennsylvania. That's straightforward to underwrite but offers no liquids upside when NGL prices are strong.

Southwest Pennsylvania and West Virginia panhandle wells producing into the wet gas window generate ethane, propane, and other liquids alongside methane, and those liquids sell against a different pricing structure than dry gas. When NGL prices are favorable relative to gas, wet-gas Marcellus royalty checks can meaningfully outperform dry gas checks even at similar total production volumes, which is worth understanding before comparing your own statement to a neighbor's or a national average.

sections.title: The New York question
sections.html: New York state banned high-volume hydraulic fracturing in 2014, which means Marcellus minerals under New York counties along the Pennsylvania border are effectively stranded from development under current law. If you own minerals in a New York county near the productive Marcellus fairway, it's important to understand that no amount of nearby Pennsylvania activity changes your own development prospects unless the state policy changes, and any offer you receive should be evaluated with that reality front and center rather than assumed pricing based on cross-border activity.

sections.title: Legacy leases and post-production deductions
sections.html: Appalachian leases signed during the early Marcellus boom years, roughly 2008 through 2012, often included royalty terms and post-production cost deduction language that has become a genuine point of dispute in Pennsylvania and West Virginia courts since. Deductions for gathering, compression, and processing can take a meaningful bite out of gross royalty value before you ever see a check, and the specific language in your lease determines how much the operator is entitled to deduct. Reviewing your actual lease terms, in addition to your check, is worth doing before any sale conversation.

sections.title: What a listing process surfaces in a split market
sections.html: Because dry gas and wet gas Marcellus interests attract somewhat different buyer specialties, putting your interest in front of multiple buyers rather than accepting the first offer helps ensure you're reaching a buyer who actually understands your specific gas composition and deduction structure, rather than one pricing off a basin-wide average that doesn't reflect your actual net income.

sections.title: Pipeline takeaway and the basis question
sections.html: Appalachian gas production grew so quickly during the Marcellus boom years that pipeline takeaway capacity struggled to keep pace for a stretch, creating real basis differentials between what producers in some parts of Pennsylvania and West Virginia actually realized at the wellhead versus national benchmark pricing. Additional pipeline projects completed over the past several years have eased some of that constraint, though capacity and differential pricing still vary meaningfully by county depending on which specific takeaway infrastructure serves your area. It's a factor worth asking about directly, since two neighboring counties can see different effective netbacks purely based on which pipeline system their gas moves through. It's a detail easy to overlook when comparing your check to a relative's in a nearby county, but it can explain a meaningful part of the gap, and it's a fair question to raise with any buyer whose offer seems to be pricing your gas at a national benchmark rather than your actual realized price.

faqs.q: Is wet gas Marcellus acreage worth more than dry gas?
faqs.a: It often nets more per unit of production when NGL prices are strong, since liquids sell at a premium to dry gas alone, but this varies with commodity price cycles rather than being a fixed rule.

faqs.q: Can I sell minerals I own in New York state under the fracking ban?
faqs.a: Yes, ownership can still be sold or leased, but current state law prevents high-volume fracturing development, which limits near-term value compared to Pennsylvania or West Virginia acreage.

faqs.q: Why is my royalty check smaller than the gross value implies?
faqs.a: Post-production cost deductions for gathering, compression, and processing are common in Appalachian leases and can significantly reduce net royalty income; your specific lease language controls how much can be deducted.

faqs.q: Which operators are most active in the Marcellus right now?
faqs.a: EQT holds the largest overall position, with Coterra, Range Resources, Antero, and Expand Energy also running significant programs across different parts of the play.

items.name: Utica Shale Mineral Rights
items.meta: Utica minerals in eastern Ohio counties like Belmont, Monroe, and Guernsey sit beneath the Marcellus at a different pressure regime. Here's what matters.

sections.html:
Ohio's Utica Shale gets compared to the Marcellus constantly because they sit close together geographically, but the two plays behave differently enough that treating them as interchangeable will cost you.

The Utica Shale sits underneath eastern Ohio, generally deeper than the overlying Marcellus, and reaches into western Pennsylvania and West Virginia as well, though Ohio hosts the most concentrated horizontal development. Belmont, Monroe, and Guernsey counties in Ohio's eastern reaches form the wet gas and condensate core, while the play turns drier to the west. Ascent Resources and Encino Energy are the two largest operators, with EQT and Gulfport also holding meaningful acreage.

sections.title: A deeper, higher-pressure target than the Marcellus
sections.html:
Because the Utica sits below the Marcellus in the same general geography, wells targeting it run deeper and typically require higher-pressure completion designs. That raises drilling costs relative to a shallower Marcellus well nearby, which is part of why Utica development has stayed more concentrated in its highest-return counties rather than spreading as broadly as the Marcellus has across Appalachia.

Some operators have drilled Utica and Marcellus laterals from the same well pads, targeting both formations from a shared surface location, which is worth knowing if you're trying to understand why a single pad site near your property might be associated with multiple lease offers referencing different formations.

sections.title: The wet gas core and why it draws the most interest
sections.html: Belmont and Monroe counties, along with parts of Guernsey, sit in the Utica's most liquids-rich window, and that NGL content has been the main driver of operator interest here relative to drier Utica acreage further west or into parts of the play extending toward Pennsylvania. If your minerals sit in this eastern Ohio core, you're in the part of the play that's drawn the most consistent operator commitment and buyer competition over the past several years.

sections.title: Ohio's mandatory pooling and unitization rules
sections.html: Ohio, like Oklahoma, allows for mandatory unitization of minerals into a drilling unit under certain conditions, administered through the Ohio Department of Natural Resources. If your family's interest has been swept into a unit through this process rather than a voluntary lease, it's worth understanding the specific unitization order terms, since they set your royalty rate and can differ meaningfully from what a voluntarily negotiated lease in the same county might have secured.

sections.title: Comparing offers in a two-formation county
sections.html: Because eastern Ohio counties frequently have both Marcellus and Utica potential under the same tract, it's worth confirming exactly which formation any offer or lease is referencing before comparing numbers to a neighbor's deal or a published county average. A broker who separates the two plays clearly when evaluating your interest, rather than blending them into one number, is going to give you a more accurate picture of what you actually own.

sections.title: Point Pleasant as the specific target within the Utica
sections.html: Most of the horizontal drilling described broadly as Utica development actually targets the Point Pleasant interval at the base of the Utica formation specifically, a distinction that matters more to geologists than most mineral owners but that shows up in how operators describe their acreage and results. This zone tends to be thicker and more consistently productive in the play's core eastern Ohio counties than the overlying Utica shale proper, which is part of why development has stayed concentrated in a fairly defined geographic core rather than spreading broadly across the formation's full mapped extent. If you're comparing well results or offers against a neighbor's, confirming both interests reference the same specific target zone avoids comparing genuinely different things, and it's a reasonable question to put directly to any buyer citing offset well performance as justification for their number. The Ohio Department of Natural Resources publishes well-level production data that breaks out formation and target zone, so this is verifiable rather than something you have to accept on a buyer's word alone, and checking it before you negotiate puts you on more even footing, especially when the offer you've received cites strong nearby results without specifying which formation those results actually came from. Getting that specificity in writing protects you if the actual well results turn out to be less impressive than described.

faqs.q: Is the Utica Shale the same as the Marcellus?
faqs.a: No. They're separate formations, with the Utica sitting deeper and requiring higher-pressure completions; they're sometimes drilled from the same surface pads but priced and evaluated separately.

faqs.q: Which Ohio counties are considered core Utica acreage?
faqs.a: Belmont, Monroe, and parts of Guernsey County sit in the liquids-rich core that has drawn the most consistent operator and buyer interest.

faqs.q: What is mandatory unitization in Ohio?
faqs.a: It's a process allowing operators to include minerals in a drilling unit under state approval even without a voluntary lease from every owner; unitization order terms set the applicable royalty rate.

faqs.q: Who are the largest Utica operators right now?
faqs.a: Ascent Resources and Encino Energy hold the largest positions, with EQT and Gulfport also active in parts of the play.

items.name: Barnett Shale Mineral Rights
items.meta: Barnett Shale minerals in Tarrant, Denton, Johnson, or Wise county are mostly legacy production now. Here's a realistic look at what your interest is worth.

sections.html:
The Barnett was the play that started the modern shale boom, and it's now the clearest example of what happens on the other side of one. If you own minerals here, honesty about that matters more than optimism.

Mitchell Energy proved horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing could produce commercial gas from the Barnett Shale under Fort Worth in the early 2000s, and the rush that followed made this the most drilled urban shale play in American history. Tarrant, Denton, Johnson, and Wise counties still carry thousands of producing wells, many drilled fifteen to twenty years ago and now sitting deep into their decline curves. New drilling has slowed to a trickle, and most of what's out there is legacy production, not a growth story.

sections.title: Why new drilling largely stopped
sections.html:
Shale gas wells decline steeply in their first few years, and Barnett wells are no exception. Once operators had drilled the best locations across the core Tarrant and Johnson county acreage, and once cheaper, more productive plays like the Marcellus and Haynesville opened up for gas-focused capital, there was little economic reason to keep drilling new Barnett wells at scale. Many of the original operators sold out, merged, or exited entirely over the past decade, and today's Barnett operators are mostly smaller companies managing existing production rather than chasing new locations.

That doesn't mean the basin is worthless. It means the value proposition has shifted from growth to steady, declining cash flow, and any honest conversation about selling should start there. The largest original Barnett players — Devon, XTO before its Exxon acquisition, and Chesapeake in its earlier form — have all either exited or dramatically scaled back their Fort Worth-area presence, leaving behind a landscape of smaller operators managing what's left rather than chasing what's next.

sections.title: The urban drilling wrinkle
sections.html: One thing that sets the Barnett apart from almost every other basin covered here is how much of it was drilled directly under a major metropolitan area. Wells sit under neighborhoods, near schools, and close to commercial development across Fort Worth and its suburbs in a way that essentially no other US shale play replicates at this scale. That urban footprint brought its own set of local ordinances and setback rules over the years, which further limited where new wells could realistically be permitted even when operators had appetite to drill them, adding another structural reason new activity stayed rare here even during years when gas prices firmed up elsewhere.

sections.title: What your check actually reflects at this stage
sections.html:
If your Barnett wells were drilled in the 2005 to 2010 window, which covers most of the core development, they've likely settled into a long, shallow decline that could continue producing modest volumes for years or decades to come, just at a fraction of their peak rate. This is actually a reasonably predictable income stream — the steep early decline is behind you — but buyers pricing a purchase will apply a real discount for the fact that there's little to no upside from new drilling to bid the price up.

It's worth pulling several years of statements rather than a single recent one, to see where your specific wells sit on their decline curve before you talk numbers with anyone.

sections.title: Setting realistic expectations for an offer
sections.html:
The Barnett isn't going to draw the kind of multi-buyer bidding war that an active Permian tract does, and it's important to walk into any conversation with clear eyes about that. The buyer pool here consists mostly of smaller funds and individual investors specializing in mature, cash-flowing legacy interests rather than large acquisition desks chasing growth plays. A fair offer in this basin is priced against your actual trailing production and reasonable decline assumptions, not against speculative future drilling that isn't coming.

That said, thin bidding is still bidding. Getting even two or three quotes rather than accepting the first one you receive is worth the modest effort, since smaller buyers in a quiet market can vary meaningfully on how they price the same decline curve.

sections.title: When holding makes more sense than selling
sections.html: For an interest producing steady, low-decline income with no urgent need for a lump sum, simply continuing to collect royalty checks can be the more sensible path, particularly since Barnett wells that have already survived a decade or more of production often keep producing small volumes for a long time yet. Selling makes the most sense when you need liquidity now, want to simplify an estate with many small fractional owners, or have reason to believe the specific well nearest your tract is close to plugging.

faqs.q: Is anyone still drilling new wells in the Barnett Shale?
faqs.a: New drilling has slowed dramatically compared to the 2005-2010 boom years; most current activity is limited maintenance or occasional infill work rather than large-scale new development.

faqs.q: Why would I sell a mature interest instead of just collecting the royalty?
faqs.a: Selling makes sense if you need cash now, want to simplify a fractional-interest estate, or believe your specific well is nearing the end of its economic life; otherwise continued royalty income can be the better path.

faqs.q: Will I get multiple competitive offers on Barnett minerals the way I might in an active play?
faqs.a: The buyer pool is smaller than in active shale plays, but getting more than one quote still matters, since smaller specialized buyers can price the same production data differently.

faqs.q: How do I know where my well sits on its decline curve?
faqs.a: Pull several years of royalty statements rather than a single recent one; the trend line tells you far more about remaining value than any single month's check.

items.name: Niobrara Mineral Rights
items.meta: Niobrara Chalk minerals outside Weld County's developed core, across eastern Colorado, Wyoming, and Nebraska, are a more speculative, less proven position.

sections.html:
The Niobrara Chalk gets its name recognition from the tightly developed DJ Basin core, but the formation itself extends across a much wider, far less proven stretch of the plains.

The Niobrara Chalk and Marl is the formation that underlies the DJ Basin's core Weld County development, but it extends well beyond that established area, spreading across a broader stretch of eastern Colorado, Wyoming, and western Nebraska. Outside the densely drilled DJ core, this formation has seen scattered, exploratory-stage interest rather than the sustained multi-well-pad development that defines Weld County proper, and it's important for owners in these outer areas to understand that distinction clearly rather than assume DJ Basin activity levels apply to their tract.

sections.title: Why the formation behaves so differently outside the core
sections.html: Chalk and marl thickness, natural fracturing, and pressure regime all vary considerably as you move away from the thickest, most productive part of the Niobrara under Weld County. Wells drilled in these outer extension areas have produced genuinely mixed results — some operators have found economic production, others have drilled dry or marginal wells and moved on. That inconsistency is the core reason this remains a speculative, exploratory-stage position in most areas rather than a proven development play.

sections.title: Nebraska and Wyoming: even less development history
sections.html: Nebraska's Niobrara acreage has seen only limited horizontal test drilling over the years, generally without triggering the kind of sustained follow-on development that would establish a clear production trend. Wyoming's portion of the formation, separate from the state's Powder River Basin activity, has seen similarly sparse interest. If your family's minerals sit in either state under Niobrara-prospective acreage, it's realistic to expect this to remain an undeveloped or lightly tested position for the foreseeable future absent a specific operator announcing plans nearby.

sections.title: What an offer on undeveloped Niobrara acreage actually reflects
sections.html: Because there's limited nearby production data in most extension areas, offers on undeveloped Niobrara minerals outside the DJ core are inherently more speculative and should be evaluated as such. A buyer offering to purchase this kind of position is generally betting on future exploratory success rather than paying against known, proven production, which is a fundamentally different transaction than buying a producing DJ Basin interest, and the price should reflect that speculative nature honestly on both sides.

sections.title: Deciding whether to sell speculative acreage or hold it
sections.html: For owners of undeveloped Niobrara minerals outside the proven core, selling now locks in a modest but certain amount for a position that might otherwise sit undeveloped for years, while holding preserves optionality if an operator eventually tests your specific area successfully. Neither choice is inherently wrong; it depends on your own tolerance for a long, uncertain wait against a smaller but immediate payout.

sections.title: Reading the difference between a lease offer and a mineral sale offer
sections.html: In speculative acreage like much of the outer Niobrara, it's common to receive a lease offer, which pays a bonus for the right to explore and produce over a set term without transferring your underlying ownership, rather than an outright purchase offer for the minerals themselves. These are fundamentally different transactions, and it's worth being clear on which one you're being asked to sign. A lease preserves your long-term ownership and royalty upside if a well is eventually drilled successfully, while a mineral sale converts your entire position, including any future upside, into a single payment today. Neither is automatically the better choice, but confusing the two can lead to giving up more than you intended. Reading the actual document title and the granting clause language before signing anything is the simplest way to avoid this mistake, and any legitimate buyer or lessee should be willing to walk you through exactly which transaction they're proposing. If a company representative seems reluctant to clarify this distinction plainly when asked, treat that reluctance itself as useful information about how the rest of the deal is likely to go, and don't hesitate to walk away and ask someone else the same direct question. A little patience here tends to serve owners better than settling for the first number offered.

faqs.q: Is Niobrara acreage outside the DJ Basin core the same value as Weld County minerals?
faqs.a: No. The formation extends well beyond the established DJ core, but outer areas have seen far less development and much more variable well results, making them a genuinely different, more speculative position.

faqs.q: Has Nebraska seen real Niobrara development?
faqs.a: Only limited horizontal test drilling has occurred there historically, without establishing a sustained development trend, so most Nebraska Niobrara acreage remains lightly tested.

faqs.q: Why would a buyer want undeveloped, unproven Niobrara minerals?
faqs.a: They're generally betting on future exploratory success in a specific area, which is a speculative transaction rather than a purchase against known production.

faqs.q: Should I hold undeveloped Niobrara minerals or sell now?
faqs.a: That depends on your tolerance for an uncertain, potentially long wait for development versus taking a smaller, certain amount now; there's no universally correct answer.

items.name: Powder River Basin Mineral Rights
items.meta: Powder River Basin minerals in Campbell, Converse, or Johnson county Wyoming were called the next Permian. Here's what actually happened and what remains.

sections.html:
A few years back, this basin was pitched hard as the next major oil discovery in America. The results came in more modest than the marketing did, and mineral owners deserve the honest version.

The Powder River Basin covers northeastern Wyoming and a small piece of southern Montana, with Campbell, Converse, and Johnson counties in Wyoming forming the areas of most recent horizontal drilling interest. The basin has a long legacy of coalbed methane production stretching back decades, layered beneath newer horizontal targets in the Niobrara, Mowry, Turner, and Frontier formations that drew significant industry attention starting around 2016.

sections.title: The coalbed methane legacy underneath everything
sections.html: Long before the recent horizontal oil interest, the Powder River was one of the country's largest coalbed methane producing regions, built on shallow, low-cost wells targeting thick coal seams. That CBM boom peaked and declined over the 2000s and 2010s as gas prices weakened and the best coal acreage was drilled out. If your family's minerals have a long production history here, there's a good chance a meaningful part of it traces back to that earlier CBM development rather than the newer horizontal oil wells.

sections.title: What the 'next Permian' pitch actually produced
sections.html:
Starting around 2016, several operators drilled ambitious horizontal test wells in Converse County targeting stacked Niobrara, Turner, and other benches, and some industry commentary drew comparisons to the Permian's multi-bench stacking. Results were genuinely mixed — some wells performed well, others underwhelmed relative to the initial excitement, and the basin never saw the sustained, broad-based development pace that comparison implied. Devon and Chesapeake's successor Expand Energy have continued more selective drilling in the strongest parts of Converse County, but at a fraction of the pace early projections suggested.

This matters for mineral owners because it means development near your tract, if any, is likely to be more targeted and slower-paced than a hot shale play elsewhere, and buyer offers should reflect that more measured reality rather than lingering hype from years-old headlines.

sections.title: Where activity is still real versus where it's gone quiet
sections.html: Core Converse County acreage in the strongest benches still sees selective drilling and remains the part of the basin with the most active buyer interest. Campbell County, historically the heart of the CBM boom, is now mostly legacy production with limited new horizontal activity. Johnson County and the basin's outer extent see even less current development. Knowing specifically where your tract sits relative to this uneven activity matters more here than in a more uniformly active basin.

sections.title: Evaluating an offer against realistic expectations
sections.html: Given the gap between early hype and actual results, it's worth being skeptical of any offer that seems to be pricing your minerals as though the basin were still in its 2016-era excitement phase, and equally worth pushing back on a lowball offer that ignores the genuine, if selective, drilling still happening in Converse County's core. A broker who can point to actual recent permits and completions near your tract gives you a much more grounded basis for negotiation than either extreme.

sections.title: Wyoming's split-estate and checkerboard land pattern
sections.html: Much of the Powder River Basin sits within a historical checkerboard land pattern left over from nineteenth-century railroad land grants, mixing private, state, and federal ownership in an alternating section-by-section grid across parts of the basin. Combined with common split-estate situations where surface and mineral ownership were severed generations ago, this creates a genuinely more complex permitting and access landscape than a basin with more uniform private ownership. If you're trying to understand why development has moved unevenly across seemingly similar-looking acreage nearby, this patchwork land history is often a bigger factor than the geology itself. Confirming exactly what your family's deed conveys, and whether the surface above it is under the same or different ownership, is a worthwhile step before assuming any offer accurately reflects your actual position. Wyoming's Oil and Gas Conservation Commandate and the Bureau of Land Management both maintain records that can help sort out which pattern applies to your specific section.

faqs.q: Did the Powder River Basin turn out to be the next Permian?
faqs.a: No. Early horizontal test results generated significant industry excitement starting around 2016, but development has been more selective and slower-paced than that comparison suggested.

faqs.q: Is coalbed methane still a factor in Powder River Basin mineral value?
faqs.a: For many long-held interests, yes — a significant share of historical production traces back to the earlier CBM boom rather than newer horizontal oil wells, and much of that production is now in long-term decline.

faqs.q: Which counties still see active horizontal drilling?
faqs.a: Converse County's strongest benches remain the most actively drilled part of the basin; Campbell and Johnson counties see comparatively little new horizontal activity today.

faqs.q: How do I know if an offer is pricing my minerals fairly given the basin's mixed track record?
faqs.a: Ask for the offer to reference actual recent permits or completions near your specific tract rather than basin-wide reputation, whether that reputation is optimistic or overly cautious.

items.name: DJ Basin Mineral Rights
items.meta: DJ Basin minerals in Weld or Adams county sit inside Colorado's tightened permitting environment. Here's what that means for buyer demand and timing.

sections.html:
No basin covered here has had its development so directly reworked by state regulation the way the DJ has. Understanding Colorado's permitting shift is not optional if you own minerals here.

The Denver-Julesburg Basin sits primarily under Weld and Adams counties in northeastern Colorado, extending into parts of Wyoming and Nebraska, and produces from the Niobrara chalk and the underlying Codell sandstone. Chevron, through its acquisition of Noble Energy, and Civitas Resources are the dominant operators in the current core, alongside a smaller Occidental position. This basin was one of the most active in the country through the mid-2010s before Colorado's regulatory environment changed the pace and geography of new permitting.

sections.title: What changed with Colorado's setback rules
sections.html:
Senate Bill 19-181, passed in 2019, shifted oil and gas regulation in Colorado toward prioritizing public health and safety in permitting decisions and gave local governments more authority over drilling within their jurisdictions. Combined with expanded setback distances from homes and schools, this made permitting near populated areas of Weld and Adams counties slower and more contested than it had been. Operators responded by consolidating development into large, comprehensive drilling plans covering hundreds of wells at once, submitted and reviewed as single packages rather than piecemeal permits.

For mineral owners, this means activity near your tract may now depend heavily on whether it falls inside one of these large comprehensive area plans, which are public record through the Colorado Energy and Carbon Management Commandate and worth checking directly.

sections.title: Where development is still concentrated
sections.html: Despite the regulatory shift, core Weld County acreage away from the densest residential development remains genuinely active, with large multi-well pads still being permitted and drilled under the comprehensive plan structure. Adams County and areas closer to the Denver metro corridor see much more limited new activity given proximity constraints. If your minerals sit in outer Weld County agricultural land, your development outlook looks meaningfully different than if you're in a more populated corridor.

sections.title: How this affects buyer appetite
sections.html: The regulatory complexity has thinned the buyer pool somewhat compared to less-regulated basins, since acquiring DJ Basin minerals requires understanding both the geology and Colorado's permitting process to underwrite confidently. That said, buyers who specialize in this basin are still actively competing for producing and near-term-development interests in the areas covered by active comprehensive plans. Undeveloped acreage outside those approved plans draws a noticeably smaller and more cautious buyer field.

sections.title: Selling into a basin with real political risk
sections.html: Colorado's regulatory trajectory has been a real variable for years now, and any responsible valuation of DJ Basin minerals should account for the possibility of further permitting changes rather than assuming the current environment is fixed. A broker who tracks Colorado's rulemaking alongside the geology can help you weigh whether current buyer offers are pricing that risk fairly, or whether waiting for more clarity on a specific comprehensive plan near your tract makes more sense before selling.

sections.title: The Codell as a secondary bench
sections.html: Beneath the Niobrara chalk that gets most of the attention, the Codell sandstone provides a secondary, thinner target that operators in the DJ Basin core have frequently developed alongside or after their primary Niobrara wells on the same pad. Where both benches are economic, a spacing unit can support more total wells than a single-formation basin would, which matters for how much long-term development potential remains under a given tract. Not every part of the basin has commercial Codell potential, so it's worth asking whether your specific section has seen or is expected to see this secondary development before assuming your unit's drilling is complete once the primary Niobrara wells are in. Comprehensive area plan filings with the state commandate generally spell out which benches an operator intends to target, so this is verifiable rather than guesswork if you're willing to pull the actual filing, and it's worth doing before assuming a single Niobrara well represents the full extent of what's coming to your unit, particularly given how much long-term value a second bench can add to an otherwise fully drilled section.

faqs.q: Does Colorado's SB19-181 mean drilling has stopped in the DJ Basin?
faqs.a: No. Development continues, particularly in outer Weld County, but it's now routed through large comprehensive area plans rather than individual well-by-well permits, and pace near populated areas has slowed.

faqs.q: How do I find out if my tract is inside an approved comprehensive plan?
faqs.a: The Colorado Energy and Carbon Management Commandate publishes comprehensive area plan boundaries and status; a broker can check your specific section against current filings.

faqs.q: Is Weld County still worth owning minerals in?
faqs.a: Core outer Weld County acreage remains actively drilled by Chevron/Noble and Civitas; value depends heavily on whether your tract falls within an active development plan.

faqs.q: Should I worry about future Colorado regulatory changes affecting my sale?
faqs.a: It's a reasonable factor to weigh. Colorado's oil and gas rules have shifted meaningfully in the past decade, and that history is worth discussing with a buyer or broker who tracks the state's rulemaking.

items.name: San Juan Basin Mineral Rights
items.meta: San Juan Basin minerals in New Mexico or Colorado sit over declining coalbed methane and a newer, more selective Mancos Shale oil play. Here's the split.

sections.html:
This basin has two very different stories running at once: an old coalbed methane play winding down, and a newer, more selective oil play that hasn't fully proven itself yet.

The San Juan Basin spans northwestern New Mexico and southwestern Colorado, with San Juan and Rio Arriba counties in New Mexico and La Plata County in Colorado forming its core. It was one of the country's largest coalbed methane basins through the 1990s and 2000s, and more recently operators including Ovintiv, formerly Encana, and WPX have tested horizontal Mancos Shale oil development layered above the older coal seams.

sections.title: The coalbed methane legacy
